turns.speaker: Narrator
turns.text:
In the making of the episode you’re about to hear, we recorded a call between a founder and investors, where the founder made this huge pivot because of COVID-19 and now she’s absolutely crushing it. Which was surprising, and impressive. But then the subject of software patents came up and the investor started getting all riled up about the ways in which a patent can hurt a startup.
I thought patents were supposed to protect a startup. I had no idea. Anyway, the call was super interesting so we decided to turn it into its own special episode for Pitch+ subscribers.
It features investors Sarah Downey and Phil Nadel who are very passionate about patents. The episode is live right now, and it’s available for Pitch+ subscribers only. Just go to pitch.show/plus and sign up to get ad free listening, plus special episodes like the one we published today. Called “The Patent Trap”
Okay, coming up after this: How are the startup founders who called into our show at the beginning of the pandemic, doing now?
[break]
Is it even possible for startups to succeed in a pandemic? This was the question on our minds when COVID-19 started body slamming the economy. And so back in April and May, we let founders call-in and get advice from investors.
Well, here we are now in August. We’re 5-months into this pandemic, and we began wondering about the founders who called in months ago. Are they doing any better now? Or are they worse off?
So producer Max Gibson and I decided to call them back and see how it's been going since last spring.
We learned the good, the bad, the ugly of running a startup the last few months. And what’s great about these callers, is how radically different each of their experiences have been.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Hey Max.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Hey Josh.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So who’s first?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Okay, so first up we have Ben Snyder. He has a company called Lumineux Chocolate. They make chocolate...

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Oh, “bean to bar chocolate,” is that what he called it?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Exactly, right. They were like totally relying on in-person tastings. But then they were planning on opening right in March, which obviously, we know what happened there.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yep. So his question for investors was like, “What do I do now?” And Charles was like, “Hey, why don’t you just send your chocolate to people in the mail and do virtual tastings?” Like you could literally put little bars of chocolate in envelopes.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Here is what Charles and Elizabeth said to Ben in that call-in show back in the spring.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Is it possible to sort of make that sampler experience something that the consumer could try and home at a cost that's not prohibitive to you but that would give them some sense for the product? I know a number of wineries that are doing that right now, too, and it seems to be working out pretty well, it seems to be popular.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And frankly speaking, being in California, I wouldn't be able to go in person. You can actually reach a market that you wouldn't have been able to have reached before.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Hey, Ben.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Hey.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So, uh, did you follow their advice?

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: I did. So we were able to do virtual tastings. We started that shortly after that episode aired. We had three tastings within a month, and…

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Tell me about that. When you do a tasting, what is that?

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Yeah, so they would be able to go on our website, and then they were able to buy a chocolate tasting kit. It was five bucks. And they got a small sampling of all six of our varieties of chocolate, along with a notes sheet. And then we had an Instagram live session, and we would taste the chocolates one at a time with everybody on the Instagram live, so everyone would be able to taste it with us. And the best part was people were able to tell us the flavors that they were getting from the chocolate, what they liked and didn’t like about the chocolate. And it was really a fun time.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: That's cool. So how's, how's the company been doing?

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Things have been going really well. Right after that episode aired on The Pitch, it was amazing the support we got from other listeners of the show. In the two weeks after that episode aired, we had over two thousand dollars in sales just from people saying that they heard us on The Pitch.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: That's awesome.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Yeah, so that was great, but since then sales have been going well. We have been growing 50 percent month over month.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: What are you up to now in sales?

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: At this point since the end of March? We're at almost 11,000 in sales.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: How much sales had you done before then? Before you called in?

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: One hundred.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: One hundred dollars?

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Dollars, dollars.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: I mean that’s incredible. You started a business and got to 11,000 dollars in sales during a pandemic.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Thanks, Ben. Thanks for giving us the update.

turns.speaker: Ben
turns.text: Thanks a lot, Josh. It's great to talk to you.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Thanks, Ben. Bye.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: I mean it’s great to hear things are going so well, you know.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yeah. I love that so many listeners ordered his chocolate. That's amazing. I guess I'm not the only person who heard that and was just like, “Damn, I could go for some bean to bar chocolate right now.”

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: You are a hungry host, you know.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: [laughs] Alright, next caller.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Next up, we have Laura Alotaibi. Venues N More is her business.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Birthday parties and stuff for people. Right?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yes. Yeah. And then obviously events stopped happening.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Right. No more events. Sounds familiar.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: And the investors were like, yeah, “Can the clown join a Zoom call and scare all the children that way?” That kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: You know, they actually suggested that.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Like the one thing I remember from that call-in was their just relentless optimism during like the most horrific time for businesses.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: This is Elizabeth and Charles again.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: It's funny, as you were describing this very seemingly bleak situation. I was actually thinking “this is so exciting.” You actually have a lot of amazing opportunities ahead of you.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: Like even when things return to normal, if you can crack this digital piece, I wouldn't be surprised if it ends up becoming a chunk of your business even once things snap back to normal.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Laura, so I'm curious to hear, like, how - did you follow their advice and how did it work out?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: I was very excited. And then once I heard, you know, the optimism, I definitely jumped on board. The first thing I did is I reached out to my most active vendors online that I knew were pivoting. I said, “Look, let's try it out. Let's post these online listings.” And I had a lot of optimism. And so we have like a princess that can Zoom with you and read a book to you for a birthday party, which is kind of cool.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: And we have a DJ that can do like a trivia night with you and your friends, or he can do a dance party via Zoom.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So you just took that relentless optimism and just passed it on.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yes, that's what happened.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: How many of those virtual events did you do in total?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: You know, to be honest. We only had three bookings through the site.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Ah.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah. And I thought that there would be more interest. But I still think it's... it's still a new idea for people to...

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: I mean, like, it sounds like it was advice that you got amped about in the room and were like pretty on board with. But like, it didn't actually pan out.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: You know, I don't think so, because I think that people can jump on Zoom and celebrate, right? And so they're not thinking about, “How do I differentiate that Zoom call.”

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: And so even friends will come to me like, “Oh, I'm celebrating a 50th birthday party, but it's gonna be via Zoom, what can I do?” And I was like, “You know hire this DJ and have a dance party.” I mean that would be amazing. But, you know, people don't think about it, right?

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: How do you dance with someone virtually?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Josh, I've seen it done. Believe me.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Does it work?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: It works. It works, yeah

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: It's fun.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Wait, wait, you’ve experienced this Max. You've done a virtual dance party?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: I have experienced this. Yeah. Clubs have been hosting them and they kind of like cycle through whoever is being highlighted at the moment. So like some people get featured as like the dancer. It kinda incentivizes you to keep moving, you know.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: It's like when you get featured on the Jumbotron at the baseball game.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Exactly. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Okay. That actually does sound fun. So you're saying, like you just think you were too early, but like, you think virtual events, like, are gonna be a thing in the event world, like you think eventually, like people are going to get tired of regular Zoom calls, and they’re gonna wanna spice things up.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: How's your business doing right now, though?

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: So, you know, it's, it's kind of in the same situation that it was in March. Bookings are almost non-existent now. I can't really control what's going on outside, but I can control Venues N More. Just really staying optimistic, stay focused on the goals. I’m going to keep focusing on the online events and really waiting for the event industry to open up, because I think 2021 is gonna, it’s gonna be the year.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: All right. Well, thank you so much for checking in and letting us know the update.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: All right, thank you.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: Laura
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Oof, that’s tough. If only I had a dollar for every optimistic comment from a founder.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yeah, gosh.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: I’d be loaded.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: So next up, we have Chris Murphy. Chris is the owner of Brewella’s.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Brewella’s.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yes, yeah, the coffee shop in Cleveland.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Not our normal fare on this show, but...

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: No, indeed not.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: And he was like, I can't open up my coffee and crepe shop. Should I sell on DoorDash or Uber Eats and...

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: The investors were like, “Do whatever you can to survive, man.”

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: I know they were very serious. It was a little startling.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: It was sobering. I remember. Do you want to play us any of that sobering tape?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yeah, I do. Here it is. This is Sarah and Phil.

turns.speaker: Phil
turns.text: You know, when I hear about your business I’m just afraid of what the restaurant business is going to be like, even post covid. Right? So first, I think there's going to be a trend where people are going to continue to be afraid to go into restaurants for some time. And I think small restaurants are going to have a really tough time making it.

turns.speaker: Sarah
turns.text: If I were you, I would research hard what it would take to get on Uber Eats, DoorDash or one of these platforms. And I think that's really what it is, is like survive until things get back to normal. Unfortunately, nobody knows how or when. But like, you know, if you need to convert more to delivery for now, even if it's not a great business model, if it keeps you alive until you can do your thing again, like do what you need to do.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Chris, that was probably the most sobering advice anyone received on that call-in.

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: What did you think of that?

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: I was like, OK, so this is a little different than I'm sure like the conversations usually go. There was a minute where I was like remembering, you know, who I was talking to and how much, you know, what kind of companies they usually work with and, but to be completely honest, there was a sense after where it was like this, like, oh, well, it's going to be like really hard and like, good luck. And it was like, yeah, I know it's gonna be really hard, but I actually feel like I have some ideas that might make it work. And the big word I took away from that thing was like how to survive basically through it.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So when did you open back up?

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: I was off for about a month. We had the shop completely closed. And then from that point on, I opened up in very, very small steps.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Uh-huh.

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: So we took all the tables out, so there was no seating. There was just an in lane and an out lane. So then we opened the coffee bar back up, just to kind of get a sense of how to get people in and out. And what I kind of took away from that, and noticed actually after, was customers weren't really scared to come back in. People did come in asking when we would put tables back in there, people were asking when we were gonna add food back, if we're gonna have our full menu. I had to be very patient and like slow compared to the people that were coming into the shop for a good amount of people.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Oh wow.

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: And then a big thing for us here, though, was it was very difficult to mandate masks. Our county hadn't done it. Our state hadn't done it. It was basically on us, on the businesses in the city to start mandating this mask policy. So that was kind of like a frustration for me that I was the one again having to like, supply all of this.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So the advice you got from the investors to strongly consider delivery services like Uber, Uber Eats and DoorDash, even though that's going to take a significant chunk of your margin… Did you follow the investors advice?

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: So I, I didn’t think it was the answer to how we were gonna long term survive. Whereas a bigger restaurant, which might have, you know, 15 to 20 employees, a full kitchen, things like that, yes, I think that that’s much easier to pivot into this delivery method. But for us and for a cafe, I mean coffee doesn’t really travel well. A lot of the reason of a cafe is like you think of the conversations you have and seeing people. And then the crepes themselves, like part of the, part of the beauty of them was people love watching them be made. People love that they get it right away. So it’s, it was kind of, it went against everything that I kind of had built up in my head of why this business had worked in the first place.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So your business is like, like, is it back to normal levels? Like, are you doing as much in sales as you were in….?

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: Oh, no.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: No?

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Are you at like 25 percent of where you were as far sales?

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: Yeah, I would say probably about 25 percent.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: If not a little bit less. But it is working. I'm definitely staying afloat. But on a positive note, we have been somewhat busy in the sense of we are only doing to go orders. I did, eventually I started putting the crepes out again, but I did a very limited menu. I started testing this idea of call ahead orders. So we’re about 50 percent call ahead and 50 percent in shop orders.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Oh, wow. You're making it.

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: I'm making it. I'm trying.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Chris, this has been a pleasure.

turns.speaker: Chris
turns.text: All right. Thank you, guys. And I'll talk to you soon, hopefully. Bye.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Bye.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Alright, who’s next?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yeah, so next we have Daniel Melendez. He has the business in Mexico City. And he had this big pivot to help waiters that were out of work find jobs with delivery platforms.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yes, yep, and I remember like the investors were super psyched about his pivot. Like they thought it could be better than his original business.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text:
We’ll take a short break here. And when we come back, we’ll call Daniel.
[break]

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Who's next?

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Great, so next we're going to talk with Daniel Melendez. He's the founder of Uno Punto Cinco.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Uno Punto Cinco.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: They're based in Mexico City. If you remember, their business was really complicated. Even the investors were confused by it in the original call. But here’s what you need to know: It's that they were working with a bunch of restaurants, specifically the waiters and waitresses in those restaurants.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Like, this is the pivot he was pitching to the investors was like, I can help all these people get work at the Mexican equivalent of DoorDash.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Right.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: And the investors were like, “That's awesome. Go do that.”

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yes, exactly. Here’s what Elizabeth said.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Right now. Your mission is to help waiters and waitresses. This very much aligns with that. You have the supply. You can make money. It makes perfect sense and I agree the delivery opportunity is there. I would just go and do that.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Daniel.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Hi, how are you, Josh? How are you, Max?

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Hey, I’m good. How are, how are things there with the pandemic?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So Mexico, as the city has already opened like for four weeks now. But people are afraid. People are afraid because, uh, the pandemic is still going on. And the hospitalization is almost at its full capacity. So most of the waiters whom we work with say, uh, “I need to choose between being healthy or having food on my table.” Because our priority in Mexico for most of the people is not, not their wellness or is not keeping their self healthy, but keeping their self eating. So, so it's pretty different.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Jeez. Well, let's talk about the business. When you called in, you spoke with Elizabeth and Charles. Did you take their advice? Like they were obviously very excited about your new idea and not so excited about your old business.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Well, I took their advice, but it didn't bring a lot of revenue to the table. In about three months, we made about two thousand dollars from that model.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: How many people right now are using that marketplace platform to get work through these delivery services?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Between 50 to 100 per week, something like that

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: And you just take like a percentage of each transaction is that how it works?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Since the end of May, we decide to give it for free because we were not making enough revenue in order to change our lives or the life of Uno Punto Cinco. And probably for a waiter that we charge 50 dollars off of his first salaries means a lot. So we decided to stop charging, and we decided to do it for free.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yeah. You did make two thousand dollars from it, but now you're not making anything.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Yeah, that's the point. We have tried several things and nothing replaced the revenue that we have. I have three months invested from my personal savings in order to keep the company alive. So yeah, right now we are... myself, I'm in an economic struggle. So that's why we’re right now, we're where we are.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: So what’s the plan, what are you going to do?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Well, right now my biggest angel investor is very insistent. He has a Colombian delivery platform. He's insisting that I should take a job with him and help him to bring my waiters to this new delivery app. He told me, “Come and work with me in my startup, invest for myself a little bit in Uno Punto Cinco and see what happens in a few months."

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Wait, so you’re saying you might take a job with someone else, and put your own business on hold?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: I haven't decided yet, but I think that I will do. I get a job, and after 6 to 12 months, we will figure out how, how or what we’re going to do with Uno Punto Cinco

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: What does it feel like being at this crossroads where you have to go back and work for somebody else in order to keep your company afloat? Does it feel like you've failed in some way?

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Actually, if I shut down right now Uno Punto Cinco, this Monday, I have a job and a job that pays me much more better than 95 percent of the Mexicans. So, yeah I feel sad. But I also think that I'm thankful for, with life, with myself, because these opportunities doesn't happen. I think that, well in Mexico, doesn't happen that often.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yeah. Thanks, Daniel.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Thank you very much for your time, and for your questions.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: I hope everything goes well and that, whatever you choose, that it works out.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Bye, thank you.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Bye

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Wow. I wasn’t expecting that.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: What weren’t you expecting?

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: I mean, I don’t know. It seemed like what he was starting had the potential to really take off, but the fact that he made it free, that’s interesting. Like it sounds like he was like these people really need the help, so we’re just gonna make it free.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: Yeah. I mean, it sounded just like a nice thing to do. Like it wasn't making the business enough money for it to make a difference in whether or not they could continue operating. So he was like, well, I guess it's providing these waiters a good service, so I’ll keep it going.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text: Yeah, I love that. Like I keep hearing about, like, little tiny stories like that about people making decisions that favor others over their own self interests. I dunno, for all the bad we see in humanity these days, it's good to be reminded of the good.

turns.speaker: Max
turns.text: And I’m sure those like waiters really appreciate it.

turns.speaker: Josh
turns.text:
I’d imagine so.

turns.text: That's what I was going to say.

turns.text: Yo.
